item.title: Permit B in Svitto: how to request and renew it
item.description: Duration 1-5 years, prerequisites and renewal deadlines. Complete guide with necessary documents and mandatory LAMal insurance.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Permit B = temporary and renewable residence for foreigners in Switzerland - Prerequisites: valid employment contract and compulsory health insurance - Managed by the cantons under federal supervision of the SEM - Duration: usually 1–5 years, renewable before expiry
## Key facts - **What**: Type B residence permit for foreigners working and residing in Switzerland - When: Required at the same time as the employment contract, valid for the period specified in the cantonal decision - Where: At the cantonal migration office of the canton of residence or place of work - Who: SEM (State Secretariat for Migration) coordinates at federal level; cantonal offices handle local applications - Essential prerequisite: Employment contract with Swiss employer - Insurance: LAMal (illness) mandatory to be taken out within 3 months of arrival
### Permit B: The legal basis of temporary work in Switzerland
The type B residence permit is one of the most popular forms of authorisation for foreigners wishing to work and reside temporarily in Switzerland. Unlike the short-term permit (type L), limited to a maximum of one year, the B permit allows a more stable renewable stay and constitutes the legal basis for many thousands of European and international workers each year.
The administrative management of permits follows a typically Swiss federalist system. The Secretariat of State ### The B permit in everyday life: Rights, obligations and access to services
The B permit is not only a bureaucratic practice, but the key that enables legal work, access to social security, payment of taxes and the right to sign rental contracts and financial services in Switzerland. Without this document, any work activity is prohibited and exposes you to administrative sanctions and possible removal from the territory.
Once the B permit is obtained, the worker becomes subject to all Swiss tax obligations. Registration to the AVS/AI/IPG (the pension system for old age, invalidity and earnings allowance) is automatic and compulsory. The contribution paid by employees is equal to 5.3% of the gross salary, to which is added an identical contribution paid by the employer, for a total of 10.6%. Alongside this, the worker is enrolled in the daily allowance (AD) and accident insurance (AC) system, with overall rates of 1.1% up to a set annual ceiling. Add to this the federal, cantonal and municipal taxes, calculated according to the three levels of the Swiss state: each canton has its own cantonal rate, and each municipality applies a multiplier on a cantonal basis.
Health insurance (LAMal) is mandatory for all residents, regardless of the type of permit. The awards are individual, vary by canton and age group, and DO NOT
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step-by-Step Procedure: How to Request It and Which Documents You Need
The request for a Permit B begins when a candidate signs an employment contract with a company registered in Switzerland. It is the employer who, except in cantonal exceptions, submits the application to the cantonal migration office of the canton where the work will be performed. In cantons with advanced digital infrastructure, the procedure takes place entirely online through dedicated cantonal platforms; in others, physical copies and attachments are still required.
The essential documents to gather include: a valid passport or an internationally recognized identity document; the original employment contract or an authenticated copy (it must clearly indicate duties, salary, hours, and duration); proof of accommodation (lease agreement, letter of hospitality from friends or family, or reservation at a temporary facility if you do not yet have a fixed residence); the completed official application form (downloadable from the cantonal migration office website); and, for citizens of third countries, sometimes a statement from the employer attesting to the specificity or necessity of the role and the impossibility of finding candidates with work rights already present in Switzerland.
Processing times vary considerably between cantons, usually between 2 and 8 weeks. During this waiting period, the worker does not yet have the formal right to work; however, some cantons allow the start of activity 'under reservation', i.e., while awaiting the official release of the permit. This practice varies by canton and professional sector.
### Deadlines and Renewals: Don't Miss the Deadline
Once issued, Permit B is valid for the period specified in the decision (generally 1–5 years depending on nationality and contract). It is the responsibility of the worker and employer to monitor the expiration date and submit the renewal request before the deadline. Late renewal can result in periods of unlawful residence.
[Health insurance premium options vary significantly between cantons](nav:health), so it is crucial to compare the available options when registering. Health insurance is a binding prerequisite for obtaining and maintaining Permit B: without active coverage, the cantonal migration office can reject the renewal application.
If you are looking for a job offer in Switzerland, consult [the national job portal](nav:jobs) to identify positions matching your skills and sector. Many employers use this platform to recruit international talent and can provide support in completing the permit application.
### Next Steps
Identify the cantonal migration office of the canton where you intend to work and download the application forms from the official website. Contact your employer to coordinate the submission of the application. Finally, [subscribe to health insurance through the health insurance comparison tool](nav:health) before the 3-month deadline from your arrival: this is a legal obligation and a prerequisite for lawful residence in Switzerland.

item.title: LAMal Unwinding Rewards: deductibles and premium reductions
item.description: How the compulsory health insurance premiums work in the Canton of Schwyz, the deductibles available and how to claim the reduction via subsidy.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - LAMal is mandatory for all residents in Schwyz, with individual private premiums - Deductibles available: CHF 300, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 2500 per year - Cantonal subsidy reduces premiums for those with low income and limited assets
## Key facts - **What**: Mandatory health insurance (LAMal/KVG) - When: Obligation to take out insurance within 3 months of arriving in Schwyz - Where: Canton of Schwyz (premiums and subsidies managed at cantonal level) - Who: Recognized private insurers; cantonal office provides subsidies - Feature: Individual per capita premiums; not a tax or salary contribution
### Mandatory health insurance in the Canton of Schwyz
Mandatory health insurance (LAMal or KVG in German) is the foundation of the Swiss healthcare system. Anyone residing in the Canton of Schwyz—Swiss citizen or foreigner with residence permit—is required to take it out within three months of arriving in the canton. It is not a state tax, but a direct private contract with a recognized health insurance fund. Premiums are individual, calculated per person, and increase with the age of the policyholder.
LAMal premiums vary significantly from canton to canton and even within regions of the same canton. Schwyz defines its own regulatory framework and welfare policies, which reflect local choices in healthcare and fiscal sustainability. This cantonal autonomy is a characteristic element of Swiss federalism.
### Deductibles and alternative coverage models
LAMal offers six levels of deductible for adults: CHF 300, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000 and 2500 per calendar year. The deductible is the amount of medical expenses that the patient covers independently before the insurance begins to reimburse. A higher deductible entails a lower monthly premium, but means greater initial out-of-pocket expense for the policyholder in case of medical need.
In addition to the choice of deductible, insurers offer differentiated alternative models: insurance with fixed copay per medical visit, models with a general practitioner as gatekeeper for access, systems with prevention incentives. These models allow residents to choose the risk-premium trade-off most convenient for their economic situation and health profile.
[Discover how the LAMal premium calculator works](nav:health) ### Cantonal subsidy and premium reduction
Premium reduction (subsidy) is a cantonal instrument to guarantee insurance access for those with limited economic capacity. The Canton of Schwyz, like every Swiss canton, provides a contribution directly to the citizen or transmitted to the insurer, reducing the premium burden. It is a direct social subsidy, not a tax deduction on the tax return. LAMal premiums remain private amounts, never deductible from the taxable income of the Direct Federal Tax (DFT) or cantonal taxes.
The subsidy calculation depends on net family income, the number of dependents, and declared assets. Lower incomes correspond to more generous subsidies. The typical formula applies a coverage percentage (from 10% to 100%) to the individual LAMal premium: with income slightly below the threshold, the subsidy covers approximately 10-20% of the premium; with very low income, it can reach 100%.
### Eligibility criteria and subsidy validity
The eligibility criteria vary each year and are set by the cantonal administration of Schwyz based on available resources and political priorities. In general, the right arises when income falls below certain thresholds published by the Canton. The thresholds consider family composition: parents with one or more children have higher income thresholds compared to singles. Assets (savings accounts, non-agricultural real estate) are assessed: those with significant savings might not be entitled to the subsidy even with low income.
The subsidy is retroactive from the first day the applicant should have been entitled to it, generally from when income fell below the cantonal threshold. The office calculates the arrears and pays it together with future payments. The duration is set for 12 months. At the end, it is necessary to renew the application by providing updated documentation.
### The role of cantons in premium reduction
Every Swiss canton manages its own premium reduction system with full autonomy. There is no single national guideline. Geneva, Jura, and Appenzell Ausserrhoden have historically had generous systems with broad premium coverage; other cantons adopt more selective criteria. This diversity reflects the political priorities of each community and their respective available fiscal capacity.
The Confederation and the Federal Office of Social Insurance (FOSI) define the regulatory framework for LAMal (guaranteed minimum benefits, premium transparency), but cantons remain fully responsible for subsidies to ensure affordable costs. This principle of subsidiarity is a structural pillar of Swiss federalism.
[Check the cost of living and subsidies in your canton](nav:cost-of-living)
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### Step-by-step procedure to request premium reduction
**1. Verify eligibility** Before submitting an application, check whether your family income falls within the cantonal threshold set by the Canton of Schwyz for the current year. The thresholds are published online on the cantonal administration website, in the Health or Welfare section. Calculate the net income from the previous fiscal year and consider the number of dependent children and marital status (no assimilations, only official documentation). Many cantons provide an online pre-screening calculator.
2. Gather required documentation The competent cantonal office typically requires: - Federal and cantonal tax declarations for the previous year (complete and certified copy) - Recent bank statements for current and savings accounts (last 3 months) - Certificate of residence issued by the municipality (no more than 3 months old) - Copy of the LAMal insurance contract in force or insurance number - ID document and, if foreign, copy of residence permit (L, B, or C) - If unemployed: certificate of registration with the employment office or payslip from the last month worked - If self-employed: tax and accounting documentation for the previous fiscal year
3. Submit the application to the cantonal office Contact the competent cantonal office of the Canton of Schwyz (Department of Health or Subsidy Office). Methods of submission: - In person at the office during public reception hours - By certified or registered mail (recommended to have proof of receipt) - Online via the cantonal portal, if available
Always keep a copy of the application and the receipt or confirmation of receipt.
4. Waiting for the result and notification The cantonal office will examine the application within 30-60 days from receipt of complete documentation. It will notify you in writing: - Decision of approval or rejection - Monthly subsidy amount (if approved) - Period of validity (generally 12 months from the month of commencement) - Instructions on payment methods (direct to the policyholder or insurer)
If the application is rejected, the decision includes the reasons and appeal periods (usually 30 days) with the competent cantonal authority.
5. Annual renewal and notification of changes The subsidy is valid for 12 months. To maintain it, you must renew the application annually with updated documentation (new tax declaration, current bank statements). If your income, assets, number of dependent children, or marital status change significantly during the year, notify the office immediately: the subsidy may increase, decrease, or cease, with retroactive effect from the date of change.
### Practical tools and complementary considerations
Use [the LAMal premium calculator](nav:health) to estimate the monthly cost based on your age, chosen coverage model (deductible), and canton. This tool helps you understand which deductible is convenient and to plan your health care budget.
If you are unsure about eligibility, contact the Schwyz cantonal office directly: many offices offer free telephone advice. You can also contact your municipality, which often has information on subsidies and cantonal procedures.
If you change your LAMal model during the year (for example, from a CHF 500 deductible to CHF 1000) or change your insurer, notify the cantonal office of the change: the subsidy remains valid and adapts automatically to the new premiums, without loss or interruption of the benefit.

item.title: Wages and labour market in URIs
item.description: How are salaries determined in URIs? Discover sectors, levels of training, collective agreements, taxation and social security in the Swiss Alpine canton.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - In Switzerland there is no federal minimum wage; some cantons set it separately by law. - Max 45 hours/week (industry/offices); min 4 weeks vacation; AVS/AI account for 5.3% of salary. - Three-level taxation (federal, cantonal, municipal); LAMal premiums vary by canton and include subsidies.
## Key Facts - **What**: Factors that determine wages and employment in the Swiss labor market - Where: Uri Canton, central Switzerland - Contributions: AVS/AI/IPG 5.3% employee; AD/AC 1.1% up to annual ceiling - Hours: 45 hours per week maximum (industry/offices); other sectors up to 50 hours - Vacation: 4 weeks minimum per year (5 for employees under 20 years old) - LAMal: Mandatory health insurance; per capita premiums with cantonal subsidies
### Factors affecting salaries in Uri
The labor market of Uri Canton follows federal and cantonal principles that regulate wages, hours and pensions throughout Switzerland. Although Uri is not among the cantons with its own legislative minimum wage (federal law does not provide for a national minimum wage), salary depends on several factors: level of education, economic sector, collective labor agreements (CCL) in force and the cantonal tax regime.
For those working in Uri, some common national thresholds apply. The maximum working hours are set at 45 hours per week for industry, offices and commerce; other sectors can agree up to 50 hours. Minimum vacation is four weeks per year, five for employees under 20 years old. Contract terminations follow precise timelines: 1 month during the first year, 2 months from the second to the ninth year, 3 months from the tenth year onwards.
Pensions constitute a significant item in gross salary. Contributions to social security funds (AVS/AI/IPG) amount to 5.3% of salary for the employee and 5.3% for the employer; unemployment insurance (AD/AC) accounts for 1.1% up to an annual ceiling. The occupational pension fund (LPP/BVG), when applicable, varies by age: from 7% for ages 25–34 up to 18% for ages 55 and over (until the reference age).
Health insurance (LAMal/KVG) is mandatory for all residents in Switzerland and is not applied through salary, but through individual premiums paid directly to insurance companies. Premiums vary by canton and region and benefit from cantonal reductions (subsidies) for medium-low incomes.
### Taxation and collective labor agreements
Taxation significantly affects net salary. Three levels of taxes operate in Switzerland: federal (the same throughout the country), cantonal and municipal. Uri has its own cantonal multiplier and municipalities apply a multiplier on the cantonal rate; this cascading structure affects the net amount that the employee actually receives.
Many economic sectors operate under collective labor agreements that set sector minimum wages, hours and benefits. Not all sectors have a CLA: membership in an employers' organization or trade union that adheres to a CLA determines whether the worker benefits from these protections. Identifying the applicable CLA for your sector is essential to understand contractual rights and obligations.
Beyond technical factors, Uri's labor market is influenced by its geographical position in Swiss alpine territory and the canton's economic dynamics. Some sectors may offer more employment opportunities than others, just as levels of education determine access to better-paid positions. To determine the exact salary and taxes due in Uri, it is advisable to consult the [online calculators](nav:calculator) provided by federal and cantonal administrations. ### Evaluate the contractual conditions in Uri
When moving or changing jobs in Uri, the first assessment is about the level of training and experience required. A high nominal salary can be deceptively low once taxes, contributions and insurance premiums are deducted. A worker receiving a gross salary often finds that the net is significantly lower when the three tax rates (federal, cantonal, municipal) and social insurance contributions are subtracted.
In URI, as in all of Switzerland, a first discriminant between contracts is the adherence to a collective labour agreement. If your employer is a member of an employer association that adheres to a CCL in your industry, the contract is subject to federal and sectoral minimum standards: hours, holidays, night/holiday supplements, salary supplements are already defined. An individual contract, by contrast, requires case-by-case negotiation and leaves fewer protections established by law or agreement.
### Social security and taxes: the impact on net income
Compulsory social security (AVS/AI) weighs directly on the salary: 5.3% is automatically paid from the paycheck; the employer pays an additional 5.3%. Unemployment insurance (AD) is another 1.1% until a ceiling is reached. If your contract includes an LPP/BVG fund, the contribution varies by age group and can reach 18% for workers over 55.
Direct taxes
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Concrete steps to start working in Uri
Before accepting a job offer in Uri, gather information on three fronts. First: verify the applicable collective labor agreement (CLA) in your sector by contacting the trade union or employer; the CLA defines sectoral minimum wage, working hours, benefits and forms of protection. Second: calculate the tax effect using the SECO calculator or the Uri tax office; enter the proposed gross salary and immediately discover your monthly/annual net income. Third: check LAMal premiums for your profile (age, gender, franchise) by visiting the official comparison tool and verify if you are entitled to cantonal subsidies.
When signing the contract, ensure it contains the start date, net/gross amount, duration (definite/indefinite), weekly hours, days of leave, probation period and termination clauses. If the contract refers to a CLA, request a copy of the applicable text. Keep the documentation: it will be useful for future verifications and for any disputes with the employer.
### Registration, taxes and deadlines
Within 3 months of arriving in Uri, register with the municipal residence authorities (population office). Registration is mandatory and opens access to cantonal public services. At the same time, you must register with a [LAMal](nav:health) health insurance fund; you can do this online or by directly contacting an insurance company.
If you are a tax resident in Uri as of December 31, you are subject to federal, cantonal and municipal income tax. The federal tax return usually expires on March 31 of the following year; Uri may have its own deadlines. Keep pay slips, receipts and pension documents to support your return.
If you have an LPP/BVG (occupational pension) contract, the fund sends annual statements: verify them for correctness of contributions and reserved balance. The amount of the pension at the reference age (65 years for men, 64 for women, with possible variations) depends on the accumulated capital and the conversion rate of the fund.
### Useful contacts and online tools
To navigate the Uri labor market with awareness: - SECO for job offers and information on the national market - Uri tax office for tax returns and advice - [Official LAMal comparison tool](nav:health) for premiums and cantonal subsidies - Uri pension office for information on AVS, LPP and subsidies - [Salary calculator](nav:calculator) for net-to-gross simulations
Using these tools from the early stages of your job search allows you to compare offers realistically and plan your budget in Uri.

item.title: AVS and complementary services in Canton Uri
item.description: How the first pillar works in Canton Uri: compensation fund, pension calculation, contribution gaps and supplementary benefits for the minimum living wage.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Mandatory first pillar: 5.3% employee salary contributions - Uri Compensation Fund collects payments and calculates AVH annuities - Contribution gaps: recoverable through additional payments - Supplementary benefits cover the minimum living allowance if insufficient income
## Key facts - **What**: First pillar (AVS) managed by cantonal clearing house - When: Contributions paid throughout the working life; reference age pension - Where: Canton Uri; UFAS offices for federal matters - Who: Employees, employers, freelancers (each contributes their own %) - Rate: 5.3% of salary for employees; 5.3% employers; 10.6% self-employed - Protection: Complementary services for those who do not reach a vital minimum - Institution: BSV (Federal Office of Social Insurance) coordinates at federal level
### The first pillar in Canton Uri
In Canton Uri, as in all Swiss cantons, the first pillar of social security (AVS) represents the basis of the protection system for old age and disability. The cantonal compensation fund, a federal body at regional level, is responsible for the collection of compulsory contributions and the calculation of annuities.
AVS contributions follow a precise pattern: employees pay 5.3% of their salary, employers an identical percentage (5.3%), while the self-employed pay 10.6% of their income. This structure ensures that funding ## Complementary services: the role in the protection of the vital minimum
In Canton Uri, the supplementary benefit system (CCP) acts as a safety net for policyholders whose AVS annuity is not sufficient to cover basic living expenses: housing, food, healthcare, utilities. CCPs are paid in conjunction with the AVS annuity, to supplement it up to the level of the vital minimum. The amount varies depending on the personal situation (single person, couple, households with children) and the actual regional costs in the canton.
It is not a fixed amount universal benefit: each case is evaluated on the basis of concrete need. Those who receive an AVS annuity close to the limit but still insufficient can apply for CCPs to bridge the gap. The recognition is automatic if the application is submitted correctly and the documents are complete.
### Combination AVS + LPP + complementary performance
The first pillar (AVS) is flanked by the [secondo pilastro (LPP, Cassa pensioni)](nav:pension), which collects contributions from employees and employers in proportion to the coordinated salary. LPP contributions vary by age group: - 25–34 years: 7% - 35–44 years: 10% - 45–54 years: 15% - 55 years and over: 18% (up to the reference age)
When the first and second pillars together do not reach the ** vital minimum **, the CCPs intervene. Those who have integrated with a third pillar (3a) further strengthen their protection, even if it is not mandatory.
### Practical procedure in the Canton
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## How to verify your contributions and request supplementary benefits
The first step is to verify your contribution record with the compensation fund of Canton Uri. You can obtain an extract (contribution account) by presenting yourself directly at the counters or by requesting the documentation by mail. The extract shows year by year the registered payments, any gaps, and the number of accumulated contribution years.
If there are gaps in the extract, the fund informs about the deadlines for recovery. The retroactive payment of missing contributions must be accompanied by an invoice from the fund itself with an amount indexed according to federal directives. The terms for recovery are limited: it is not possible to recover gaps of more than five years without proven reasons of force majeure.
### Application for supplementary benefits: step-by-step
**1. Verify eligibility**: The AVS pension (plus any other pension from LPP, third pillar, or private policies) must not cover the minimum cost of living in Canton Uri. If the sum is lower, you have the right to submit an application.
2. Gather documents: Extract your UFAS account from the federal portal (e-service authentication), obtain your AVS pension certificate from the Uri cantonal fund, and prepare a detailed statement of monthly expenses (rent with contract, health insurance premiums, utilities, food).
3. Complete the application: Download the application form from the Canton Uri administration website. There are no unified federal forms; each canton has its own administrative procedure.
4. Submit: Send the application by mail or deliver it to the competent counter. Check the deadline: usually the application must arrive before December 31st for recognition of the previous year.
5. Settlement: Within 30–60 days from the complete application, if everything is in order, the benefit is recognized and monthly payment begins.
### Online tools for calculation and monitoring
The [salary and tax calculator](nav:calculator) allows you to simulate social deductions (including AVS/AI/IPG), but for an accurate estimate of your future pension, it is advisable to contact the compensation fund of Canton Uri directly. UFAS also offers on the federal portal (www.ufas.admin.ch) an online contribution data extraction service through e-service authentication with a Swiss digital certificate. This is the quickest way to obtain your contribution account without having to travel.
For questions about the contribution recovery procedure, specific gaps, or your future pension situation, the compensation fund remains the main point of contact: it understands local dynamics and can advise on the best completion strategy. Consult the [AVS and pension calculator](nav:pension) for an initial estimate of your expected pension.

item.title: AVS and complementary services in canton Uri
item.description: Compensation fund, pension calculation and contribution gaps in the first pillar: how URI supplementary benefits work
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - First pillar (AVS): the cantonal compensation fund calculates the pension based on contributions paid during the career - Contribution gaps: periods without payments reduce the amount of the final pension - Complementary benefits: supplement the AVS annuity up to the vital minimum if insufficient
## Key facts - **What**: First Pillar of Swiss Social Security (AVS/AHV) managed at federal and cantonal level - Where: Canton Uri, like every Swiss canton, has a compensation fund - Who: Uri Cantonal Compensation Fund; UFAS (Federal Office of Social Insurance) - Contributions: 5.3% employee salary, 10.6% total with employer - Retirement age: 65 years old men, 64 years old women (since 2025)
The first pillar of Swiss social security, known as AVS (Old Age and Survivors Insurance) or AHV in German, represents the basis of social protection for those who live and work in Switzerland. In the canton of Uri, as in any other jurisdiction, the cantonal compensation fund plays a central role in the calculation and payment of the old-age pension. This institution collects contributions from workers and employers, manages tax records, and determines the monthly benefit amount upon retirement.
### The role of the clearing house
The Uri cantonal clearing house is not an autonomous body, but operates according to the federal rules established by the UFAS. Each ### How the compensation fund calculates the annuity
The cantonal compensation fund of Uri follows the federal pension calculation mechanism. The system is based on two main elements: the amount of contributions paid during the working career and the number of years of contribution recognised.
For each year of contribution, the cash register records the amounts paid. These contributions are indexed according to the evolution of the Swiss average wage, which means that payments from past years are adjusted upwards to take into account wage inflation. At the time of retirement, the fund calculates the average income over the last 15 years and, from this, determines the annual income according to federal rates.
Contribution gaps have a direct impact on this calculation. A gap of a full year results in a percentage reduction in annuity. In Uri, as everywhere in Switzerland, gaps can result from: - Periods of unemployment not covered by unemployment insurance - Sickness or temporary disability - Voluntary interruptions of work for training or personal reasons - Self-employment without compulsory payments - Periods of care for dependent family members (in some cases managed through remediation contributions)
### How to Redeem Tax Gaps
Some gaps can be filled through voluntary payments, called redemptions. The Uri Compensation Fund provides advice on
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### What to do before retirement
Several years before reaching retirement age (65 for men, 64 for women from 2025), it is advisable to verify your contributions statement from the Uri canton compensation fund. This document shows a summary of all payments registered during your career and identifies any gaps. Many citizens discover forgotten or incorrectly recorded periods at this stage, and have the opportunity to request corrections.
The concrete steps are as follows:
1. Contact the Uri canton compensation fund to request your contributions statement (the service is free) 2. Review the document to identify periods without contributions or with reduced contributions 3. If there are gaps, evaluate whether to buy them out (calculate the costs and benefits of the solution) or accept them and plan supplementary benefits 4. Approximately 3-6 months before retirement, submit your old-age pension (AVS) application to the compensation fund
The Uri canton compensation fund also provides an estimate of your future pension during the pre-retirement phase, useful for concretely planning the transition to retirement and for assessing whether supplementary benefits will be necessary.
### Requesting supplementary benefits
If the estimated old-age pension (AVS) is insufficient compared to the minimum living standard established in Uri canton, it is important to submit an application for supplementary benefits to the competent Uri canton office. Municipal administrations have dedicated counters or centralized cantonal offices. The procedure requires:
1. Completion of an official application form (provided by the competent Uri canton office) 2. Documentation of income situation (most recent tax documents, income certificates, bank statements) 3. Complete documentation of assets (real estate, savings, other income sources) 4. Assessment by the cantonal office (timeframes vary, typically 4-8 weeks) 5. Notification of the decision and start of monthly benefit payment
Supplementary benefits are financed by cantons and municipalities and do not need to be repaid. However, the right to benefits depends on verification of your financial situation: if your assets or income increase beyond the established thresholds, benefits can be reduced or revoked.
### Practical tools and resources
For those who want to learn more about calculating their pension, there is a [salary and pension calculator](nav:pension) available, which allows you to simulate amounts based on your personal data and work history. Additionally, the [tax return declaration](nav:tax-return) can provide information on the income documentation required for supplementary benefits applications.
Stay updated on pension system reforms and important deadlines: subscribe to the Frontaliere Ticino newsletter to receive updates on old-age pension (AVS), pensions, taxation, and cost of living in Switzerland.

item.title: Ireland also sends Dubliners back to Italy
item.description: Ireland adheres to the policy of repatriation of asylum seekers. Seventh European country, after Switzerland, to adopt this strategy.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Ireland adopts a policy of repatriation of foreigners to Italy - Seventh European country, after Switzerland, Germany, Austria, Sweden, Finland and the Netherlands - New AMMR procedures in force from 12 June 2026 with reduced time
## Key facts - **What**: Repatriation of asylum seekers to the EU country of first arrival - When: From 12 June 2026 (AMMR in force) - Where: To Italy mainly - Who: Irish Government, Home Office and Migration - Countries: 7 European countries including Switzerland - Standard: AMMR Regulation (Asylum Management and Migration Regulation)
Ireland also joins the countries that intend to send migrants back to Italy as a country of first arrival. The news is reported in the media. It is the seventh country - after Germany, Switzerland, Austria, Sweden, Finland and the Netherlands - that will adopt such a policy with respect to so-called "dublinantes", migrants awaiting asylum who are in a European country other than the one of entry.
A spokesperson for the Irish Ministry of Home Affairs and Migration said: 'Ireland continues to comply with and process all notifications, requests and transfers to all Member States, including Italy, under the Asylum and Migration Management Regulation (AMMR) or the previous Dublin III Regulation, as applicable.'
### Who are the Dubliners
The so-called "Dubliners" are asylum seekers who are in a European country other than ### Implications for Switzerland
Switzerland has already adopted this policy, positioning itself among the first European countries to implement the system of repatriation of foreigners to Italy. This means that when an asylum seeker arrives on Swiss territory after having transited through Italy, the Swiss authorities (SEM - Secretariat of State for Migration) assess the situation according to the criteria of the Dublin III Regulation or AMMR. If the first access to Europe took place in Italy, the applicant can be repatriated to that country for the examination of the application. Ireland's decision to join this policy represents a convergence at European level, although it is nothing new for Switzerland, which has already experimented with return mechanisms for years.
### How times change with AMMR
The new AMMR Regulation introduces simplified criteria and reduced time compared to Dublin III. The procedures for determining the competent State will be faster. An asylum seeker who arrives in Switzerland knowing that they are from Italy must be aware that the repatriation process could be accelerated from 12 June 2026 onwards. Eurodac biometric documents facilitate the identification of the initial migration route, allowing authorities to coordinate transfers in a timely manner.

## In a nutshell - The Canton of Lucerne applies taxes on inheritances and donations according to cantonal law - The rates vary according to the degree of kinship of the heir - Spouse and children have subsidized tax regimes - The declaration of succession has precise deadlines established by the canton
## Key facts - **What**: Cantonal inheritance and gift tax levied by the Canton of Lucerne - Where: Lucerne cantonal tax administration - Who declares: Heirs and successors of the deceased person - When: Within the terms established by the cantonal legislation of Lucerne - Key factor: The rate depends on the degree of kinship (spouse, children, parents, others)
In Switzerland, inheritance and gift taxation is regulated at the cantonal level: there is no uniform federal tax in this area, but each canton — including the Canton of Lucerne — independently manages the taxation of inheritances and transfers of assets. This principle of fiscal decentralisation is central to Swiss federalism and means that rates, exemptions and procedures can differ significantly from canton to canton.
The Canton of Lucerne, like all Swiss cantons, applies a progressive taxation system based on the degree of kinship of the heir to the deceased. This means that those closest to the deceased (spouse, children) generally benefit from reduced rates or exemptions, while distant collaterals and unrelated ones are One of the most important factors in determining inheritance tax in the Canton of Lucerne is the heir's degree of kinship. This is not merely a bureaucratic technicality: it forms the foundation upon which the entire cantonal tax structure is built.
### Variations by Heir Category
When applying inheritance tax, the Canton of Lucerne first classifies heirs into well-defined categories. Each category corresponds to a set of rates that gradually increase as the relationship moves away from the immediate family nucleus. A surviving spouse, in many cantonal systems, pays no tax or a minimal percentage. Children, regardless of age, are typically placed in a class with very low rates. The deceased's parents, if still alive, fall into an intermediate class. Siblings are in a higher class. Cousins, aunts, uncles, and unrelated individuals face an even heavier tax burden. This 'step-like' structure is intentional: legislators recognize that closer family ties deserve greater tax protection.
### Taxable Base Calculation
Tax is calculated on the net value of the inheritance—the deceased's gross estate minus debts, funeral expenses, and other deductions authorized by cantonal law. It is not levied on the entire abstract estate, but rather on the share that each individual heir actually receives, based on that specific heir's degree of kinship. This means two siblings inheriting from the same parent might pay different rates if one is domiciled in the Canton of Lucerne and the other in another canton, as some cantons tax non-residents on real estate within their territory.
### Lifetime Donations by the Testator
Alongside inheritance tax, the Canton of Lucerne also regulates gift tax—transfers of assets made during the donor's lifetime, rather than upon death. In many Swiss cantons, gifts are taxed at identical or very similar rates to inheritance tax, though there may be a 'cooling-off period' (a number of years within which the gift 'counts' for tax purposes). The rationale is clear: legislators do not want to allow asset owners to circumvent inheritance tax by gifting property just days before death. Consequently, many cantons treat gifts made in the final years of life as part of the inheritance. For details on gift tax planning in the Canton of Lucerne, consult our [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). Inheritance declaration is a mandatory administrative procedure in Switzerland. It is not optional: anyone who has inherited assets in the Canton of Lucerne has a legal obligation to declare the inheritance within the deadlines prescribed by Lucerne cantonal law.
### Deadlines
The timing of the declaration is critical. Generally, in Swiss cantons, heirs have a defined period (typically 3, 6, or 12 months from the death, depending on the canton) to notify the competent tax office of the inheritance. In the Canton of Lucerne, this deadline is established by the current cantonal law. Missing the deadline may result in administrative penalties, including late declaration fines. It is important to emphasize that the date of the testator's death is the reference date for tax calculation (the so-called 'status quo at the time of death'). The value of inherited assets is generally determined at the market price on the date of death.
### Required Documentation
To declare an inheritance in the Canton of Lucerne, you will typically need to provide: official death certificate; will (if it exists) or documentation on intestate succession; inventory of inherited assets (real estate, bank accounts, insurance policies, vehicles, etc.); documentation of debts and liabilities; identification details of all heirs; domicile declarations of the heirs (important for determining tax jurisdiction). Check the official Canton of Lucerne website for available submission channels. For complex cases — inheritances with assets in multiple cantons, conflicts between heirs, foreign assets, or intricate tax situations — it is advisable to consult a tax advisor or notary specializing in inheritance law.

item.title: Mute Federal Council on Climate: Mazzone calls for a course

The central theme of her speech? The Federal Council's inaction in the face of the heatwaves of the past summer, which left gaps in decisions and concrete measures for Switzerland's climate. 'The Federal Council must remove the environment department from Albert Rösti,' stated the Geneva native, addressing the federal government directly. According to the Greens' president, the Swiss executive has clear responsibilities and must 'change course' in a radical and immediate way. The demand is broad and incisive. Mazzone stressed that the Federal Council must 'put climate first,' 'adopt urgent measures to adapt our cities and countryside,' and 'invest heavily in climate protection by ending the harmful dependence on fossil fuels.' Words that summarize a vision of profound transformation of federal policy. ### The government's silence on the summer heatwave The core of the criticism is institutional silence. Mazzone condemned the fact that the Federal Council remained mute during the summer heatwave. Even more serious: upon returning from recess, the government's first decisions went in the opposite direction on climate. The Federal Council rejected the initiative on the sustainable financial center, which could have had a 'significant impact on the global climate,' according to the Greens' president. This contrast—absence of government communication during the extreme heat and subsequent decisions in the opposite direction—represents, for Mazzone, a clear failure of federal leadership. From her perspective, the Swiss government failed to grasp the urgency of the climate crisis even when Swiss people were directly experiencing the discomfort of heatwaves and the needs for urban and agricultural adaptation. ### Budget figures: CHF 900 million for defense, zero for climate The most significant data point for understanding the Greens' position concerns the allocation of federal public resources. According to Mazzone, the Federal Council allocated an additional CHF 900 million to the army. In the same context, it did not allocate 'a single extra franc to protect the climate.' This direct contrast—a precise figure for defense, a zero sum for climate—highlights a federal priority scale that places military defense above environmental protection. And this will impact the [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) of every Swiss resident through municipal, cantonal, and local service taxation. ### The Federal Climate Debate and the Role of DETEC The challenge that Mazzone raises goes beyond a simple ministerial reorganization: it touches the heart of Swiss federal governance and how Bern intends to address the climate crisis in the coming years in a structural way. Albert Rösti, director of the DETEC (Department of the Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications), has been a point of friction in the Swiss political debate for months. Attributing the climate dossier to a department that also manages transport, energy and communications creates priority conflicts: how to balance road expansion, rail efficiency, digital infrastructure and renewable investment with the imperative to reduce emissions and protect the climate? The Greens' position suggests that the current institutional set-up is not sufficient to ensure coherent and truly priority climate protection. If the climate is managed within a cross-cutting department, it risks being subordinated to short-term pressures from other sectors. ### Federal investments and pressure on Swiss municipalities Without climate-specific federal investments, Swiss municipalities and cantons must locally finance climate adaptation measures. ### What these choices mean for those who live and work in Switzerland

Heatwaves and droughts are not political abstractions confined to international climate conferences: they directly impact rents, food prices, energy costs, drinking water availability, quality of life, and productivity in every Swiss canton.

If the Federal Council continues to fail to prioritize specific federal investments in climate adaptation, the weight of the transition falls on multiple levels. Municipalities locally finance energy insulation, shaded parks, resilient water supply systems, and infrastructure reinforcements against floods and landslides. Employers face rising costs for climate control, workplace safety in extreme heat, and absenteeism due to thermal discomfort. Workers suffer from reduced productivity, health risks in exposed sectors (construction, agriculture, transport), and stress from climate vulnerability. Consumers see food prices remain volatile in the face of crop losses and drought management.

### How to follow the federal political debate on the climate

Mazzone's request will be debated in Swiss democratic forums in the coming months. The Federal Chambers, particularly specialized committees like the CATAE (Environment, Spatial Planning and Energy Committee), will take positions on how to redesign federal climate governance and allocate public resources.

Swiss citizens who wish to influence this process have effective tools at their disposal: follow parliamentary procedures on parlament.ch to track climate-related motions and initiatives; contact your parliamentary representatives (National Councilors and Councilors of States) to highlight local climate adaptation priorities in your cantons; monitor federal consultations when the Federal Council proposes ordinances and decrees on environmental protection and energy transition.

The articulation of the federal debate depends on the democratic pressure exerted by citizens, businesses, trade unions, and environmental organizations. The Greens' position is one piece of a broader mosaic of pushes for a more ambitious and funded central climate policy.

### An investment that requires complete planning
Those who decide to buy a house in the Canton of Lucerne face an operation that touches personal finances, cantonal taxation and federal administration simultaneously. There is no federal law that imposes a minimum percentage of own funds to buy a home in Switzerland. However, the market has developed a well-established practice: banks usually require at least 20% of the purchase value as equity. This rule is not random.
If you invest your 20%, the bank covers the remaining 80% through mortgage. item.title: Licence L Lucerne: renewal after one year
item.description: The short-term L permit is valid for up to 12 months and can be renewed. Find out how it works in Lucerne, the extension options and the transition to a residence permit.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - The L permit allows you to work for up to 12 months in Switzerland - Is bound to the employer and professional activity - The extension must be requested before the SEM expires - Possible transition to permit B or C
## Key facts - **What**: Short-term L permit (foreign SEM category) - Duration: Up to 12 months maximum from release - Who manages: State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) + cantonal administrations - Constraints: Linked to the employer and the job assignment - Transition: Possible passage to permit B (residence) or C (domicile)
The short-term L permit is a federal category of residence in Switzerland that allows foreign workers to carry out a temporary activity. The maximum duration is set at 12 months from release. The issuance and management of the permit is the responsibility of the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) at the federal level, in coordination with the cantonal administrations.
In the Canton of Lucerne, as in all Swiss cantons, the L permit is bound to the specific employer and professional activity indicated at the time of application. This means that the worker cannot change employer during the validity period without authorisation. Similarly, the activity is limited to that agreed with the SEM.
### Validity and expiration
The maximum validity of the L permit is 12 months. This duration is standardized at the federal level. However, the SEM and the authorities ## What happens during the first year
During the period of validity of the L permit, the worker must respect the established constraints and maintain residence in the Canton of Lucerne (or in the specific address registered with the authorities). The employer must immediately notify the SEM of any significant change: change of address, business interruption, office transfer.
The L permit does not automatically give access to identical social benefits to Swiss residents. The social security coverage (AVS/AI, LPP, LAMal) remains linked to the employer. Check with the employer that the correct contributions have been paid from the first day of activity, and consult the [nostro calcolatore della previdenza sociale](nav:pension) to verify your accrued rights.
### Expiry options: extension, transition, revocation
A few months after the expiration of the 12 months, the worker and the employer must decide on the future path.
**Extension of L leave **: If both parties (worker and employer) wish to continue the collaboration and the initial conditions are met, the SEM may extend the L leave for a further 12 months. There is no theoretical maximum limit for extensions, but the SEM assesses on a case-by-case basis whether the need is still temporary. After one or two renewals, the SEM may ask the employer to apply for a B permit (residence) if the employment appears stable.
Transition to permit B (residence): If the employment relationship becomes stable and lasting (from 2-3 years onwards),
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## How to renew or transition the L permit: a practical procedure
If you are about to expire your L permit and want to continue in Switzerland, here are the concrete steps to follow.
### Step 1: Evaluate the path with the employer
At least 2-3 months before the expiration date, discuss with the employer whether they intend to request an extension or convert the permit to a stable category (B or C). The employer is the official applicant, not the employee. If the employer is not willing to continue, you need to look for a new job that requires a new L permit or plan your return.
### Step 2: Prepare the documentation
For an L permit extension, the employer collects the updated employment contract (or a letter of intent to extend), certificates of salary and contributions paid in the last 12 months, a statement from the employer justifying the continuation of the temporary activity, and a copy of the current L permit.
For a transition to B, add a document attesting to the stability of the employment (a letter from the employer with an analysis of the long-term role) and employment contracts showing continuity over time.
### Step 3: Submit the application to the cantonal SEM office in Lucerne
The employer (preferably through an HR consultant or lawyer) submits the application to the competent SEM office in Lucerne. The application must be submitted before the permit expires. A late application can lead to denial, even if the procedure was already underway. Check the opening times of the counters and the accepted transmission channels (paper, digital, via post).
### Step 4: Response times
The SEM usually takes 4-8 weeks to deliberate. During this time, if the permit has formally expired but the extension request or transition has been submitted, most cantons allow the employee to continue working. However, this must be verified with the local office. Stay in touch with the employer to monitor the status of the request.
### Step 5: After approval
Once the L permit extension or transition to B/C is approved, the SEM issues a new permit. The employee will receive it by post or can pick it up at the office. Update your address with the local authorities and inform the employer of the new permit number. Check the new contribution and tax rates applicable using the [tax and salary calculator](nav:calculator).
## Practical tools and key contacts
To verify your social security rights during this transition period (AVS, LPP), use our [social security calculator](nav:pension). Do not wait until the expiration date to act. Start the request 60 days before the end of the L permit: the processing times are rigid and a delay can be costly.

item.title: Residence permit C Lucerne: complete guide
item.description: Requirements, integration criteria and application procedure for residence permit C in the Canton of Lucerne. Complete step-by-step guide.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Permit C requires 10 years residence (5 for EU/EFTA) - Specific cantonal criteria determine approval - Application to cantonal migration office
## Key facts - **What**: Residence permit (C) — permanent residence - When: After 10 years continuous residence (5 for EU/EFTA) - Where: Canton Lucerne - Who: Foreign nationals, federal management (SEM) - Duration: 10 years, renewable - Prerequisite: Documented continuous residence
The residence permit, commonly referred to as permit C, represents the status of permanent residence in Switzerland. Those who have been working or living in the Canton of Lucerne for at least ten years and meet the criteria for national and cantonal integration can apply for the change from residence permit (B) to permit C.
The federal legislation sets the clear standard: ten years of continuous residence for citizens of non-European countries, five years for EU/EFTA citizens. However, the issuance of the C permit is not automatic. Each canton applies its own criteria of linguistic, cultural and socio-economic integration. In the Canton of Lucerne, as in other cantons, the Migration Office assesses demand on the basis of combined national and cantonal parameters.
Permit C confers significantly more stable rights than permit B: protection from repatriation, freedom of movement within the Schengen area, access to social benefits, concrete possibility of ordinary naturalization after ### Rights, Duties and Integration
Whoever holds a C permit acquires substantial and well-protected rights. First of all, legal stability: they cannot be repatriated for economic or occupational reasons (for example, loss of employment). They have access to the cantonal social benefits (unemployment benefits, cantonal integration) and contribute to [federal pension programs through AVS/AI](nav:pension). They can move freely within the Schengen area for tourism or short stays. They have the right to family reunification without particular limitations, which is not guaranteed for holders of permit B.
On the other hand, the C permit is not a blank check. The holder remains subject to Swiss laws: penal, fiscal, administrative. They must pay federal, cantonal and municipal taxes. Every canton has its own tax regime, different from the others, with specific rates and multipliers. They must pay pension contributions for AVS/AI and LPP — exactly like Swiss-born citizens.
### Integration Criteria
Integration is the central node of the C permit. It is not an abstract concept: it includes concrete elements that the canton evaluates during the period of residence with permit B.
First of all, language skills. The canton usually requires a basic proficiency in the official language of the region. The exact level (A2 or B1 according to the European Framework of Reference) varies by canton and is not yet fully specified for Lucerne in this source, but it represents an important element of the evaluation.
Secondly, conduct. Absence of serious previous convictions, respect for administrative rules (payment of taxes in order, no arrears), good reputation in the local and professional context.
Thirdly, socio-economic participation. It does not mean having a minimum income fixed (Switzerland has no federal minimum wage, even if some cantons have autonomously regulated a cantonal minimum wage). It means demonstrating to be economically active or otherwise in order: employed, pensioned, rentier, student, or unemployed but regularly assisted. The local [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) influences the evaluation of the overall economic situation.
### Ordinary Naturalization
The C permit is a crucial step towards ordinary naturalization. Federal law provides: ordinary naturalization = C permit + ten years of residence (counting double the years of residence between the ages of 8 and 18) + specific cantonal/municipal requirements.
This means that whoever has obtained the C permit after ten years of residence, after another ten years with the C permit (or counting the previous years with double valuation according to age), can submit a naturalization application. The canton and the municipality examine the degree of civil and cultural integration again. Not all applicants are naturalized: the canton can refuse for reasons of insufficient integration.
### Comparison between Permits
| **Aspect** | Permit L (Short) | Permit B (Residence) | Permit C (Domicile) | |---|---|---|---| | Maximum duration | Up to 1 year | Renewable | 10 years, renewable | | Residency required | Temporary stay | Permanent situation | 10 years (5 for EU/EFTA) | | Status in Switzerland | Temporary | Intermediate | Permanent | | Geographical mobility | Limited | Switzerland | Switzerland + Schengen | | Legal protection | Minimum | Medium | Maximum | | Access to social benefits | Limited | Normal | Full |
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Procedure for application step by step
When you have reached ten years of residence (or five if EU/AELS) with a B permit, it's time to act. The procedure requires collaboration between the cantonal office and the federal SEM.
**Step 1: Verification of prerequisites**
Contact the Lucerne State Migration Office and verify that you have reached the temporal requirement. Provide continuous residence documentation: archived rental contracts, tax declarations for the past ten years, bank statements that prove continuous presence in the canton.
Step 2: Document collection
Prepare a solid and organized documentation:
- Current residence permit (B) - Extract of the federal and cantonal criminal record - Valid ID and passport - AVS contribution certification (contact UFAS/BSV) - Pay slip and employment contract (if employed), or pension/ income statement - Recent bank statement (demonstrates economic stability) - Residence certificate issued by the municipality - Language course certificates (if relevant)
Step 3: Filling out and submitting the application
The cantonal office provides an official form. Fill out the application carefully and attach complete documentation. The application is presented in person at the office or by certified mail. Keep a paper copy of everything sent.
Step 4: Cantonal investigation
The office conducts the investigation: consultation of criminal records, contacts with employer, verification with the municipality of residence, evaluation of integration. This period typically lasts three to six months.
Step 5: Communication of the decision
The office communicates the official outcome. If positive, the new permit is produced and delivered. If negative, you receive a motivated refusal notice, which can be contested within the specified terms.
### Required documents: practical checklist
Documents that can be collected as soon as possible to speed up the process:
- Valid ID or passport (with a remaining validity of at least 6 months) - Current B permit - Up-to-date residence certificate from the municipality - Employment contract and pay slips for the last 12 months - AVS contribution certification from UFAS/BSV of registration and payments - Recent bank statement (last 3 months) - Language course certificates or professional training - Letters of reference from employer or local associations
Maintaining this documentation organized and easily accessible significantly accelerates the processing of the application.
### Timelines and deadlines
There is no national deadline for submitting the C permit application. However, once the ten-year residence requirement is reached, it is advisable not to wait: the oldest candidate has a longer history to document, which facilitates the investigation and reduces the risk of incomplete documentation.
The cantonal office's decision typically arrives within three to six months from the complete application submission. If documents are missing, the office writes requests for integration, prolonging the waiting time.
Once the C permit is granted, it is valid for ten years. The renewal must be requested before the expiration date (the office sends a notice 3-4 months before the expiration date). If you change canton of residence, the C permit remains valid, but must be registered with the new canton within 14 days of the transfer.
### Concrete action: next steps
The first concrete step is to contact the Lucerne State Migration Office. Ask preliminarily what specific language integration criteria apply to the canton, which documents you should start collecting, and what the average waiting time for processing is.
If you are not yet a contributor, register with the AVS/AI and LPP registers at the employer or autonomously with the federal office. Regularly contributing to federal pension is a positive element in the evaluation of economic integration.
If your income is low, check if the canton and municipality offer sickness fund subsidies (LAMal premium reductions). This demonstrates administrative and socio-economic integration.
Finally, use the available calculators to simulate your economic balance over the next few years: this helps you plan whether the C permit application is financially convenient and ensures a conscious submission of the application.

item.description: No Swiss federal minimum wage. Discover timetables, AVS/LPP contributions, salary levels for training and collective agreements in the Canton of Bern.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - No federal minimum wage; some cantons have their own - Maximum hours 45–50 hours per week according to work sector - AVS/AI/IPG contributions: 5.3% employee salary (10.6% total) - Minimum holiday 4 weeks per year (5 under 20 years)
## Key facts - **What**: Regulatory and social security framework of the labour market in the Canton of Bern - When: Federal and cantonal regulations in force 2026 - Where: Canton Bern, central Switzerland - Who: SECO, UST/BFS, cantonal authority Bern, pension funds - Contributions: AVS/AI/IPG 5.3%, AD/AC 1.1%, LAINF/LAA 0.7–1.5% - Hours: 45 hours industry/offices; 50 hours other sectors - Holidays: Minimum 4 weeks; 5 under 20 years
The labour market in the Canton of Bern operates according to Swiss federal regulations, with cantonal and municipal specifications affecting wages, social security and taxation. Switzerland does not have a federal minimum wage, but some cantons, potentially including Bern, have established one for certain sectors. Job seekers in Bern need to understand how wage levels relate to vocational training, what mandatory contributions are paid and how the local tax system reduces the monthly net.
The Swiss training system is divided into three paths: vocational training (Federal Certificate of Competence, AFC), general training (cantonal or Swiss maturity) and tertiary training (universities, vocational colleges). Each The final tax burden on a Bern employee's salary depends on three levels of taxation: the federal direct tax (IFD), the cantonal tax, and the municipal tax. The IFD is collected by the Federal Administration; the cantonal and municipal taxes are managed by the local authorities in Bern according to their own rates. The municipal tax multiplier applies a coefficient to the cantonal tax rate, so the final tax burden varies depending on the place of residence within the Canton of Bern. These amounts do not appear as 'pension contributions' but as 'source tax' (PPC), withheld directly from the salary every month by the employer.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Procedure for Job Seekers in Bern If you are looking for work in the Canton of Bern, the first step is to identify the professional sector and the level of qualification you are looking for. The SECO publishes a national portal with job postings; in addition, national and local Bernese private portals offer opportunities. Once you receive a job offer, negotiate the salary taking into account your level of training, accumulated experience, and, crucially, the applicable CCL for your sector (if any). Ask the employer what salary ranges are for your position and compare them with what is provided for in the collective contract. If there is no applicable CCL, the salary is free but must still respect any written commitments.
Before signing a employment contract, carefully read all the conditions: working hours, holiday days, public holidays, shift supplements, and if the contract falls under a registered CCL. Verify that the proposed salary respects the minimum of the collective contract for your role and your level of experience. If the contract does not mention a CCL, the salary is negotiable but the minimum federal conditions (45-50 hours, 4 weeks of holiday, maternity/paternity) remain always valid.
### Calculation of Net Salary The gross salary you see in the job offer is NOT what you will receive: various mandatory deductions reduce it monthly. In addition to the mandatory federal contributions (AVS/AI/IPG 5.3%, AD/AC 1.1%, LAINF/LAA 0.7-1.5%), the professional pension (LPP) further reduces the amount paid. Furthermore, the federal direct tax (IFD) and the cantonal and municipal taxes of the Canton of Bern are applied through the withholding tax system (PPC). To quickly calculate the net, use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator): enter the gross, the canton (Bern), the place of residence, age, and marital status, and you will get an accurate estimate of the monthly net, as well as a detailed breakdown of all federal, cantonal, and municipal deductions.
### Deadlines, Documents, and Mandatory Registrations When you accept a job offer, the employer will provide you with a contract and guide you through the administrative registration. You must declare your definitive address in the Canton of Bern, as the municipalities calculate the payroll tax (PPC) from there. Make sure you have a mandatory health insurance (LAMal) within 3 months of starting work. If you don't have one yet, contact a health insurance company directly or contact the Bernese cantonal social welfare office, which can indicate the options with reduced premiums thanks to cantonal subsidies. The LAMal premium is your personal responsibility: the employer does not pay it nor deduct it from your payroll. The company pension fund (LPP) automatically registers eligible employees and will provide documentation on the fund and pension rights. You will receive an annual pension account extract showing the accumulated reserve value. If you want to verify the contributions and accrued interests.
### Support Tools and Next Steps Don't look for it alone: use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to simulate your monthly net for months, national portals for [job search](nav:jobs), and consult the Bernese cantonal labor office for up-to-date information on sectoral minimum wages and collective contracts. If you have specific questions about the AVS pension, the company pension fund (LPP), or the third pillar, contact the SECO or the Federal Office of Social Insurance (UFAS).

item.title: Opening a business in Bern: registration and costs
item.description: Legal forms, registration in the commercial register, administrative costs and social security obligations in the Canton of Bern
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Choice of four legal forms (sole proprietorship, simple company, Sagl, SA) with variable capital requirements - Compulsory registration in the commercial register of the Canton of Bern - Registration fees and taxes vary by form and municipality (local multiplier) - Social security obligations, health insurance and federal/cantonal tax payments
## Key facts - **What**: Opening and registering a business in the register of the Canton of Bern - Where: Municipal administration of the municipality of domicile/headquarters; competent cantonal office - Who: Entrepreneurs, self-employed, constituent companies - Legal forms: Sole proprietorship (no minimum capital), Sagl (CHF 20,000), SA (CHF 100,000) - Taxes: Federal, cantonal Bern, municipal (with local multipliers)
### The road to self-employment
Opening a business in the Canton of Bern is a decision that touches on complex fiscal, social security and administrative areas. The first choice — that of legal form — determines not only the level of personal liability, but also the costs of incorporation, accounting requirements and tax structure. Subsequently, compulsory registration in the cantonal trade register triggers a cascade of communications to tax authorities (federal, cantonal, municipal) and social security institutions. Those who do not understand these dynamics risk both administrative delays and non-tax burdens ### Initial registration fees
The administrative costs for registration in the trade register vary significantly depending on two main factors: the legal form and the municipality of seat (due to the local multiplier applied by the municipality itself).
In the Canton of Bern, each municipality applies a multiplier on the cantonal tax (direct and others). For example, a company registered in Bern pays a different multiplier than one based in a municipality in the Bernese countryside. The registration fee in the commercial register is established by the canton, but there is no single and fixed amount: it varies depending on the form and sometimes the volume of business declared.
For a sole proprietorship, costs are generally low (from a few hundred francs). A Sagl or an SA entails higher costs, not only for the registration fee, but also for the legal costs of drafting the articles of association and deeds of incorporation (if entrusted to a notary or lawyer). It is advisable to contact the trade register office of your municipality to receive an accurate quotation.
### Social security and insurance obligations
Once the activity is registered, obligations to social security and insurance institutions automatically take effect, which the owner must anticipate and manage.
If the owner hires employees, they must pay mandatory contributions: - **AVS/AI/IPG**: Employee contribution 5.3%, employer contribution 10.6% of gross salary - Unemployment
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### The concrete steps to start the activity Step 1: Define the legal form Evaluate which form (sole proprietorship, partnership, Sagl, SA) aligns best with your business model, available capital, and desired level of liability. A sole proprietorship is the fastest way to start (a few weeks). A Sagl or SA requires more time and higher costs, but offers limited liability. Step 2: Gather the required documentation Prepare with: - Copy of passport or ID card - Certificate of citizenship (ubi possidet) - Extract from the criminal register (if required by the municipality) - Statute or founding act (for companies) - Declaration on administrative positions (if applicable) Step 3: Contact the competent office in the Canton of Bern Address the municipal administration of the municipality where you have your domicile or intend to establish the activity. Ask for the official forms for registration in the commercial register (available online on the cantonal portal). Many municipalities offer information desks that guide you through the procedure. Step 4: Complete and submit the application Complete the forms accurately with company name, form, activity, domicile/seats, personal data. Attach all required documentation and the registration fee payment. Some municipalities accept online applications through digital platforms (check the website of your municipality). Step 5: Receipt of registration and tax communications Once registered, you will receive a commercial register number. You must then register with the cantonal tax administration (Directorate of Finance or equivalent in the Canton of Bern) for the cantonal tax and with the municipality for the municipal tax. The deadlines vary; the commercial register will inform you of the exact procedures. Step 6: Open a business bank account and register with social security entities Open a commercial bank account (for which you will need to show the extract from the commercial register). Contact simultaneously: - A sickness fund for the LAMal insurance (to be concluded within 3 months) - The cantonal AVS office for registration as an independent worker - If you hire employees, register with a LPP fund (professional pension) and contact an insurer for accident insurance (LAINF/LAA) **Step 7: First contribution payment After registration, you must pay the AVS/AI contributions (approximately 9.8% of the net income, with quarterly or annual payments according to the Confederation's criteria). If you have employees, the payments start from the first month of employment. ### Resources and support during the process The Canton of Bern provides online guides, downloadable forms, and information desks at the municipal administrations. The Bern Chamber of Commerce and Industry offers consultations on commercial and tax law. It is recommended to consult your municipality of domicile for an estimate of the exact local administrative costs, as they vary by municipality multiplier. Plan the timing of the registration: some obligations (e.g., opening a bank account, LAMal registration) may require 1-2 additional weeks after registration in the commercial register. Do not start the activity before completing all administrative and insurance steps. Once the activity is started, remember that operational costs do not only include initial payments. You will need to budget for annual taxes, AVS contributions, LAMal premiums, and, if applicable, LPP contributions for employees. Estimate the fiscal impact of your activity in the Canton of Bern using our [tax and salary calculator](nav:calculator). This will help you understand which federal, cantonal, and municipal tax rates will apply to your net income, facilitating initial financial planning.
